list.name: Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean
list.note: The custodians gave the strangers leave, signed their treaty in a tongue they could not read, and watched their tally ignored, Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig lapse and their hall locked. The council made in the forest at Cnoc bheag fought the war that ended the age, and now sits in Cathair dhearg with the country from the hills to every coast in its hand. It will stand its companies down in the spring and make itself a kingdom. Its ruler at the close of the age: Eilidh nic Raghnaill, speaker of Comhairle na Coille. Told of in: The council in the forest of Cnoc bheag (AE 148); The capital rises (AE 149); The lines at midsummer (AE 150); The harbour quarter changes sides (AE 150); The truce of Àth àrsaidh (AE 150); The Severance companies stood down (SE 1); The council of the kingdom seated (SE 2).

list.name: Cathair gheal
list.note: The human families left on the island, a few thousand, march north under the council's safe-conduct into the country of the old concession. Cathair gheal and Muileann àrsaidh kept out of the war; Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns. They are about to be called the Tuathaich. Ruled by the magistrate of Cathair gheal. Told of in: The northern concession (AE 20); Cathair gheal behind its walls (AE 150); Muileann àrsaidh closes its road (AE 150); The truce of Àth àrsaidh (AE 150); Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns (AE 150); The columns go north (AE 150); The Severance (AE 151); The Tuathaich homeland fixed (SE 1).

list.name: Comann an Airgid
list.note: The refiners of Muileann chiar kept their seam in their own hands through the whole age, by ledger, by compact and at last by rifle. They sold bar silver to A' Chompanaidh at their own price and paid the raiders in it for guns. Told of in: The Silver Compact (AE 44); The silver guild refuses again (AE 67); The silver guild arms (AE 148); The silver town rises (AE 150).

1.note: A strait harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd na Cloiche. The town on the wide strait took its tolls from the strangers' shipping as it had from the western pilots, and for two generations its merchants sold wool by A' Chompanaidh's weight and at A' Chompanaidh's price. When the humans' ships thinned in the years before the war, the wool piled in its warehouses and the merchants quietly began to sell inland again, against the letter of the law. By the war its harbour stood idle. The tally-book of Pike's post named its merchants the hardest bargainers on the island, since they would take only iron by weight for their wool, and they sent the first wool-ship to the humans' post in Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg's second year. Known for wool, and its idle harbour. Told of in: The pilots' double toll entered as fair (AE 3); Wool at Caol leathan (AE 5); Caol leathan's idle harbour (AE 145).

2.note: A river-island village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The river port just east of the capital stacked on its quays the coal that the barges carried down the Abhainn fhionn to A' Chompanaidh's steamships at Cathair dhomhain. In the last year of the age its townsfolk set the stacks alight rather than let a ship carry them off to burn against another Seann Toll, and the ships put in at Ros dhomhain and burned their own stores. The word reached the muster of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe at Seann Skell. Known for the coal it burned itself. Told of in: Coaling from Inis mhòr (AE 150); Word of the burned coal at Inis mhòr (AE 150).

3.note: A farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The open market town of the south-eastern farms has no walls. Its potteries took a contract in the years of the night shift for clay lamp-bodies for the night crews, thousands in a year, and the potters' own book notes that they were the first lamps made on the island for work in the dark by command. Its people kept Na Seann Spioradan through the age. Its fairs bring the south-eastern farms' grain and wool, and its potters kept working the same clay for household crocks when the contract ended. Known for the night crews' lamps. Told of in: Baile ghorm's potteries take the lamp-body contract (AE 116); Coal-lamps from Baile ghorm (AE 120).

9.note: A village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. River-island village with a landing. The Tuathaich harbour town of the north coast ate its seed corn in the second winter of Gorta Baile chrom, and was fed through that season by the kitchen of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise at the harbour, three hundred a day on fish broth and biscuit brought by sea from Cathair gheal. Its landing was walled by the humans. In the last year of the age the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lay twelve hours in a boat-shed there, heard that Strake's constables rode the western roads daily, and hired a carter of the town with a covered cart and a mule who asked nothing of what he carried. Known for the harbour kitchen of the hunger. Told of in: Inis mhin eats its seed (AE 95); The kitchen at Inis mhin's harbour (AE 95); Rumours at Inis mhin (AE 150); The carter of Inis mhin (AE 150).

10.note: A harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The river town under the red cliffs on the Abhainn uaine lives on river fish and the short ferries between its two landings. In the first spring of the war the crew-leaders of the river towns met seven men in the back room of its inn, An Cupa Dàna, gave them sealed letters and hawks cast in lead from the cartridges of Muileann chrom, and sent them north to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig; they were Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, and the boatman Coinneach Beag was among them. The ring of small river towns on the Abhainn uaine above Cathair mhòr heard the news of the war first at its inn fire, where word was turned over until everyone in the room had handled it. Known for the inn where Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe set out. Told of in: The Leaden Hawk company (AE 150); Coinneach Beag puts his name forward (AE 150); Word of Ashdown's retreat reaches Cuan dhearg (AE 150); The seven wait nine hours at An Cupa Dàna (AE 150); The lead hawks given out (AE 150).

12.note: A ford village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The ford town of the south-eastern hills, at the meeting of the Abhainn gheal and the Abhainn bhàn, sent its boatmen's sons as runners for Faire nan Lòchran in the years before the war, boys of twelve and thirteen who carried the letters from An Sligeanach Fad' às to the silver town along the causeway paths, too young for the constables to stop and too quick for a mounted man to follow. It has been a river landing since An Aois Naomh, and its boatmen's causeway paths across the flood-meadows are known to no map. Known for Faire nan Lòchran's runners. Told of in: The runners of Àth fhiadhaich (AE 142); A boy of Àth fhiadhaich at Aonghas's door (AE 142).

17.note: A river-island village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The river port of the north-east grew in the age from a fishing town into a city on the trade of the strangers. Its shipwrights learned to build in the humans' fashion for A' Chompanaidh's coasting trade, and its fishwives kept the old market on the steps where cloth was still bartered for fish long after the mark was law. In the war the townsfolk burned A' Chompanaidh's coal where it lay stacked on the quays, sooner than let it fuel one more ship like the one that shelled Seann Toll. Its barges run down the Abhainn ghorm to the sea, and in the years of An Togail its carpenters were among the men Riaghaltas nan Coigreach took for the building of the beacon towers. Known for its shipwrights, and the coal burned on its quays. Told of in: The shipwrights of Inis mhòr (AE 4); The fishwives of Inis mhòr (AE 130).

19.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the custodians' hall, its locks broken; the bridge barricaded with coal-carts in the rising; hungry since the winter, the grain shared by household. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The capital held Comhairle a' Chùraim through all the years of the strangers, and the council's roll is the spine of the age's record. Here Gormshuil nic Fhearchair and the priest Samuel Wren made the first lists of words across a table, with a cup and a loaf; here Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg was read in one tongue and signed, and here the council sat without a Ceann a' Chùraim for ten years. When Lionel Strake came Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir locked the council hall and took its keys, and the custodians sat on the floor of Macha's temple for two years. In the spring of the hundred and forty-ninth year the townsfolk broke the locks with a coal-hammer, held A' Chompanaidh's bridge with overturned carts, and fed the city from a sharing-yard behind the hall through the siege that followed. Its bells were rehung in a new frame by Torcall the mason in the first years. Tormod mac Ailein, Ceann a' Chùraim when the ships came, was buried in the town, and Artair mac Iain was seated after the chair had stood empty ten years. Known for the council roll, and the sharing-yard of the siege year. Told of in: The capital rises (AE 149); Hunger in the capital (AE 150); The rolls sent to Muileann chaol (AE 150); The Council of Custodians grants leave (AE 2); The struck line in the council roll (AE 2); Crìosd and an Eaglais written in the council roll (AE 2); The keeping of the word-list given to Gormshuil nic Fhearchair (AE 2); Wren sets his months against the moons (AE 2); Wren names the fuel of his own country (AE 2).

20.note: A hill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. The river port of the north-central country and heart of the hawk-faithful asked Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise for a copy of Wren's grammar in the thirteenth year, to read what the humans wrote of them; of all the copies that survive, theirs bears the most notes in the margins. In the war Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe slept a night in a byre near it on the road to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig. It lies on the Abhainn ìseal, and its hawk-priests kept that copy in the temple where anyone who could read the humans' letters might ask to see it. Known for the most-read copy of Wren's grammar. Told of in: The cairns of the line laid across the island (AE 6); The hawk-priests read Wren (AE 13); A hawk-priest's note beside the three words (AE 13); The hawk-priests of Cnoc bheag show Wren their margins (AE 16); The Leaden Hawk walks to the Hawk coast (AE 150).

22.note: A village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Headland village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The river-mouth city of the south coast was where A' Chompanaidh's ships loaded the coal that came down the Abhainn uaine from Seann Toll, and went out by Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich. Its fishermen netted the last salmon of the green river's mouth in the thirty-third year, a hen fish empty of eggs; the next spring none came in from the sea, their gravel under the grey slurry of the washing-floors. In the thirty-sixth year a coal ship on the ebb ran down one of its boats off the bar and did not stop, and after that the town's boats kept inshore. Known for the last salmon. Told of in: The last salmon netted at the green river's mouth (AE 33); The coal ships' lane (AE 36); A coal ship runs down a Ceann leathan boat (AE 36).

23.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The great city below the old ruin refused the mark when it was first made law, and went on paying in kind at its market for a season after the rest of the country had given in. Am Fiabhras Glas came to it in the high summer of the hundred and thirty-eighth year, and for the first time in the town's memory the market shut, stall by stall; the longest list of dead in the roll was the street of the carters. It keeps below its walls the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, and the market that refused the coin gave way at last only when A' Chompanaidh's tool-sellers would not cross its bridge for anything else. Known for the refusal of the mark. Told of in: Cathair mhòr refuses the mark (AE 18); The grey fever at Cathair mhòr (AE 138).

24.note: A headland harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. The largest of the three towns of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig has been a hawk town since the second house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig was founded there. When Lisle opened a customs house in a hired loft by its fish-steps in the forty-second year, its fishwives chased the officer out twice in his first year, and the roll says only that he went away by water. In the fever years its hawk-faithful raised a shrine to Mòd on the harbour wall itself, in open sight of the customs house. It shares its bay with Seann Skell and Ros leathan and has quarrelled with them over moorings for as long as the rolls run. Known for the customs officer who went away by water. Told of in: A customs house at Ros gheal (AE 42); The hawk-faithful carry the customs officer out of Ros gheal (AE 42); Ros gheal rows the customs officer down the coast (AE 42); The hawk-faithful of Ros gheal (AE 140); The fourth shrine stands at Ros gheal (AE 140).

26.note: A city of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. A' Chompanaidh's first warehouse, broken open for Buidhnean na Comhairle. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The deep city on the lake shore, five miles from the capital by the lake road, holds the first building the strangers ever owned outright on Dia-thìr: the stone warehouse Pike raised there in Cùmhnant Cathair dhearg's first summer to keep A' Chompanaidh's tools out of reach of the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain. A' Chompanaidh's surgeon came to its sick only once in Fiabhras nan Coigreach, and it was here that Anne Colby first wrote the dead by name. In the rising the townsfolk broke the warehouse open and carried off its rope, nails and powder for Buidhnean na Comhairle, and left its doors swinging. The fishing town runs down to the shore beside the capital's deep water, and the old folk there said the warehouse door was the first door on the island ever hung with a lock the town could not open. Known for the strangers' first warehouse. Told of in: The warehouse at Cathair dhomhain (AE 9); Cathair dhomhain joins (AE 149); The shore at Cathair dhomhain sold (AE 9); The warehouse door hung (AE 9); A' Chompanaidh's surgeon visits once (AE 59); Mòr nic Amhlaidh's counsel on names (AE 59); Colby turns the chapel into a sick-house (AE 59).

27.note: A city of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the capital's great harbour: Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir above it stripped, A' Chompanaidh's quays and deep-water quay, the burned counting-house and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's chapel; the harbour quarter opened its gates to the council. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. Ros dhomhain lies a short walk below the capital on the lake shore, and it grew in the age into a second town of sawn timber and dressed stone beside the first. Pike's trading post stood on its quay, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir on the rise above it, and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's chapel below. The mark and its hundred pence were first paid across its counter, its dockers struck beside the humans' own dockers, and the inquiry into the flood at Muileann chrom sat in Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's panelled room. In the war the harbour quarter held itself apart from both sides for a year, until its own men burned the tithe books of the counting-house by night and opened the lower gates to Buidhnean na Comhairle. Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir was found stripped at the end of an t-Sultain, its letter-books left whole on the shelves. Its quays took the coal of the hill from the barges for more than a century, and its steelyard and counting-house scales weighed every load. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's chaplains kept their register of the dead in the chapel below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and Hannah Webb's brother Daniel was shipped from its quay with the human dockers after the strike. Known for the counting-house fire and the letter-books. Told of in: The Residency above Ros dhomhain (AE 9); The Mission chapel (AE 13); The Company's deep-water quay (AE 103); The counting-house at Ros dhomhain (AE 150); The harbour quarter changes sides (AE 150); Strake forsakes the Residency (AE 150); The trading post at Ros dhomhain (AE 3); The custodians' clerk keeps a slate beside Pike's book (AE 3); The trading house's letter read at the post (AE 4); Pike's first two years balanced (AE 5); Pike writes home of the island's coal (AE 5); The chart from memory brought to the post (AE 6).

29.note: A village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The harbour on the capital shore, eighteen miles down the river from Ros dhomhain, shut the only quay it had for the coal traffic in the season of the flux and let no barge tie up; it paid A' Chompanaidh's fine from the purse that had buried its dead. Anne Colby walked there to help lay out the last of them. In Stad-oibre a' Chalaidh of the hundred and thirty-fourth year its dockers, with no human among them, refused to load the coal sent round to them; they were not shipped over the sea, but neither were they hired again for two years. Known for the quay shut against the flux. Told of in: Seann Vell's dockers stay out (AE 134).

30.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Headland village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The city of the south got A' Chompanaidh's pay office for the southern workings in the sixty-first year, when Crane moved it there from the pit-heads. The crews of every southern pit walked a day there and a day back twice a month to be paid, with no pay for the walking; Uisdean Ruadh of Muileann chrom kept the cost of it on a notched stick. Known for the pay line. Told of in: The pay office at Ceann mhin (AE 61).

31.note: A hill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The hill town south of the coal country got its pits in the thirty-seventh year, with Seumas Dubh of Raghnall Maor's crews set over them as overseer. A year later the haulage rope parted under three full tubs and crushed Coinneach Beag, a boy of eleven, and the crew killed Seumas Dubh for the haste he had ordered. A' Chompanaidh hanged two hewers, Eòin Ruadh and Fionnlagh mac Aonghais, at Ros dhomhain, the first hanging done by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach on Dia-thìr. Known for the first hanging. Told of in: Seumas Dubh set over the pits at Cnoc mhòr (AE 37); Coinneach Beag crushed on the haulage (AE 37); Seumas Dubh killed at Cnoc mhòr (AE 38); The two hanged named in the custodians' roll (AE 38).

44.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the strike town and home of Faire nan Lòchran: the walled pithead held eleven days, the book of complaints. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The pit town where the Abhainn uaine leaves the hills was the heart of the crews' own long resistance. The eleven days of its great strike in the seventy-seventh year won what the crews could win, and its roll kept Sìneag's search for an old law of rest. Its Comann an Adhlacaidh became Faire nan Lòchran, which kept a purse, a book and the copies of every petition; Eilidh nic Raghnaill led a crew there and kept the book. A' Chompanaidh walled its pithead, and in the first days of the war its constables held the walls eleven days until the well ran dry, and were marched to the coast unharmed on Eilidh's word. Sìol-lann na Companaidh built there against a stoppage was the first on the hill, and the overseer's clerk who copied the forbidden song kept his copy in its roll. Its boats have been launched at the landing since before any roll. Known for the eleven days, twice over. Told of in: The strike at Baile thais (AE 77); Leabhar Baile thais (AE 101); Baile thais walls its pithead (AE 104); The Lamp-Watch (AE 113); The siege of the store at Baile thais (AE 149); Catrìona's request to Silas Crewe (AE 77); Sìneag searches the old rolls for a law of rest (AE 77); Raghnall Breac stands his first day among the strikers (AE 77); The shrine women keep An Acair Uaine through the stoppage (AE 77); Beathag Ruadh asks Catrìona to end the stand (AE 77).

45.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Farm town with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd na Cloiche. The fishing town whose boats had anchored free at Ros dhomhain time out of mind was charged anchorage under Puingean a' Chalaidh in the twentieth year. Having paid it once, its fishermen took their catch to their own jetty and sold it there to the fish-wives who walked out from the capital and to anyone but A' Chompanaidh, whose salting-house had herring that season only from its own boats. Known for herring sold to anyone but A' Chompanaidh. Told of in: The fishermen of Baile ghlas (AE 20).

46.note: A ford village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Bhrìde. The fair ford at the crossing of the southern drove road sent its custodian Ruairidh mac Thormoid to Ceann àrsaidh in the ninety-eighth year, the eldest of the nineteen who signed the petition, born before the humans' coin was struck; he signed last and slowest. Human fishers of the concession had taught its boats to take whales with the hand-lance, and the oil went to A' Chompanaidh's lamps. It has been a resting place for herds and drovers since An Aois Naomh, and its people keep the ancestor rite of the old roads. Known for the eldest signature. Told of in: Àth fhionn signs (AE 99).

62.note: A river-island village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The river town took the eastern coal, carted over the rebuilt bridge at Ros fhionn and down to its quays, and sent it by barge to Caol chrom at the river mouth for shipping. A' Chompanaidh deepened the river at the quays in the fifty-third year, and the town's old fish market was moved to make room. Known for the moved fish market. Told of in: Coal through Inis bheag (AE 53).

63.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the last seat of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, hungry behind its walls; the last ship from the east anchored here; its human families gone north in the columns. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The citadel harbour of the western coast was the humans' western port from the earliest years, and in the autumn of the hundred and fiftieth year it became the last seat of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach, when Strake came down the Abhainn gheal with his officers and clerks and the human families of the west and south came in behind its walls. It ran short of food within weeks, and Strake ordered A' Chompanaidh's store opened to humans and townsfolk alike at one measure, with no ledger kept. The last ship from an Tìr Thall anchored off it at Samhain. Its Dia-thìrich townsfolk kept their own houses and their own market cross through three generations of A' Chompanaidh's officers at the quay, and found themselves strangers in their own gates in the last autumn. Known for the last seat, and the last ship. Told of in: Ros bheag the last seat (AE 150); Hunger in Ros bheag (AE 150); The last ship from the east (AE 150); The columns go north (AE 150); The sealed letter kept close (AE 150).

64.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. Seann Warr on the capital's western shore boils salt from the brine springs in the reed marsh behind the town, and it was the first place on the island to sell to Pike's counter, in the third year of the strangers, putting up its price when it heard what he would pay. Its carters took the salt round the lake to the capital for a century on their own roads. In the siege year it sent grain to the hills and the capital every month, by carts that went the long way round to avoid Strake's patrols. A' Chompanaidh tried twice to buy the pans outright and was twice refused, the salt-boilers holding that brine rising from the ground was no more theirs to sell than the rain. Known for brine salt, and the grain trains of the siege. Told of in: Salt from Seann Warr (AE 5).

Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The great hill city of the north-east kept the last hall of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, and Samuel Wren spent a winter there learning what the masters would teach a stranger. a generation later George Tolley shut the hall over a lecture on whether that blindness was a kind of sickness, and Seònaid nic Dhùghaill was the last of its masters to teach openly. Am Fiabhras Glas came to it at the dark of a later year, and killed the physician Riaghaltas nan Coigreach had sent. The school's last masters went on teaching under the trees of Flidais after the hall was shut, and their pupils carried the disputations to Inis bhàn. Known for the shut hall of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. 86.note: A strait harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The harbour on the low strait of the north coast has salt pans that supply the northern fisheries. The blasting-powder for the new deep galleries was landed there in the hundred and thirty-sixth year, away from the crowded southern harbours, and carted inland under guard; the custodians asked what was in the barrels and were told it was lamp-oil. It keeps the ancestor rite of the old coast, and its custodians wrote the lamp-oil into their roll with the weight the carters said the barrels had. Known for the barrels of lamp-oil. 88.note: A headland village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The walled river city on the old headland over the Abhainn fhionn sent Eachann Mòr to the council for nine years, and he lost his seat for what he said in the hall and wrote a letter over the sea. In the ninety-eighth year its custodian Aonghas Ruadh called the custodians of nineteen settlements to its hall behind the market square, and after three days of argument they set their grievance down in the petition that Peigi Ghlas carried to Ros dhomhain. In the war its companies burned the tithe-house and every ledger in it, though its custodian asked that one be spared. Its barges run down the Abhainn fhionn to Cathair dhomhain, and the custodians of the east met in its hall again in the war before the companies went out. Known for A' Chiad Athchuinge. Told of in: Eachann Mòr loses his seat (AE 50); The family of Eachann Mòr (AE 51); Eachann Mòr's first letter over the sea (AE 51); The custodians ride to Ceann àrsaidh (AE 98); Aonghas Ruadh calls the custodians of the east (AE 98); The drafting argued over three days (AE 99).

90.note: A headland harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The fishermen of the southern harbour town carried salt fish up to the camps by night in the years of Sìol-lann na Companaidh, past its ration and its rule. The custodians' roll calls it the only trade of that decade that ran the right way. Known for fish carried by night. Told of in: Fish smuggled from Ros gharbh (AE 79).

92.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. River-island village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd na Cloiche. The town a day's sail east of Baile dhìreach took in the human boatbuilders when they moved their yard there in the forty-seventh year for the timber A' Chompanaidh had promised them, and it made no joint council and no compact with them. Iain Hale refused the yard and stayed at Baile dhìreach. Within a generation the boatbuilders faded from the town's rolls. Known for the boatyard. Told of in: The boatyard moves to Inis chrom (AE 47).

95.note: A strait harbour of Cathair gheal. Its grief was loud and short, as a first grief is. Its yards took timber for A' Chompanaidh's hulls, and An Togail's officers used its quay as their first station in the north-west. Known for the wrong son. Told of in: Levy officers at Caol mhòr (AE 88); The wrong son taken at Caol mhòr (AE 88).

103.note: A river-island village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Pilgrims of Na Seann Spioradan bound for the spring of Allt an Àigh, which never failed through the three dry years, gathered at the town, and its folk fed them freely, as Na Seann Spioradan require, and opened their own granary to them rather than see them go hungry on the road home. Its wells were low, and it gave away more water than it kept. Known for the pilgrims fed. Told of in: The pilgrims' road at Inis uaine (AE 108).

104.note: A harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The river quays of the city east of the capital opened to the council's boats in the last year of the age. With them and the harbour quarter of Ros dhomhain both lost, Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir could be fed only by water, up the Abhainn gheal from the sea. Known for the quays opened to the council. Told of in: Cuan uaine opens its quays (AE 150).

105.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the old joint town of two tongues; its children of both peoples would not say which they were. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The straight town on the west coast took in the first human families to settle beside the Dia-thìrich rather than apart from them. Samuel Hale tightened herring barrels on its quay, Torcall the mason witnessed in its Dia-thìreach book, and a marriage was made there in two tongues. The town was governed for a long season by a joint council of both peoples, six of each, and lost its harbour dues to A' Chompanaidh in the years of An Togail. Thomas Hale first set his name to paper against Riaghaltas nan Coigreach here. In the last autumn each side asked the children of the old council which people they were, and most would not answer; Eilidh Hale kept the books and stayed. Its quay is a single long street down to the water, and the humans' slip where the first boat was launched stood at its foot. The storm of the wolf-moon drowned men of both peoples off its harbour in one night, and both were lit for at the lamps of the drowned. A town of both peoples at the close of the age. Known for the joint council and its children. Told of in: Baile dhìreach under one council (AE 5); The end of the joint council (AE 47); The families of Baile dhìreach (AE 150); Carpenters and a cooper come ashore at Baile dhìreach (AE 5); The rule of the shingle read to the strangers (AE 5); The compact written in both tongues (AE 5); The chair set to turn at the humans' new year (AE 5); The first council of Baile dhìreach (AE 5).

106.note: A farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. Told of in: The pox in the south (AE 40).

109.note: A chapel village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The large village on damp ground beside the sacred wood of Macha took in the orphans of the Eleven of Cnoc fhiadhaich, in a long house of stone with new thatch that its custodians made ready at the end of the street, and raised them. The wood behind it gave shelter in the last years to the priests who had left the capital's temple, and Comhairle na Coille of the war sat among its fires. The long house the custodians made ready stood at the end of the street for the rest of the age, and the orphans raised there were counted in its roll as children of the town. Known for the orphans of the Eleven. Told of in: The orphans of Cill thais (AE 27).

110.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. The greatest harbour of the south-eastern coast, where the oyster-beds lie in the shallows, loaded the silver town's bar for the coasting boats as it had since An Aois Naomh. From the forty-fourth year the guild sent all its silver south by this road, eighteen miles down the valley, and paid the custodians of the port in silver by the Muileann chiar weight on every bar. When a collier burned off the coast A' Chompanaidh's agents said at its quays that the guild had paid the raiders to do it; the charge was never proved. Torcall's crews built its new quay in the first years of the strangers. Its harbour is the largest of that coast, and in the war its custodians turned A' Chompanaidh's coasters away without a shot fired. Known for the silver road to the sea. Told of in: Seann Bhral the silver port (AE 44); The first silver carts go down to Seann Bhral (AE 44); A' Chompanaidh charges Comann an Airgid with the burning (AE 46); The cutting at Seann Bhral taken (AE 112).

113.note: A ford village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. Human fishermen of the concession taught the boats of the north-coast town to hunt whales with the hand-lance in the fifty-fifth year rather than wait for them to strand. The oil was sold to A' Chompanaidh for its lamps, and from then on whale-boats went out from the north coast every summer. Known for the whale-boats. Told of in: Whale-boats out of Àth fhionn (AE 55).

117.note: A grove village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The village of the eastern drought country had its tarn fouled by the driven cattle of every drought district within a week of the drive, and its women walked each day to the spring at Àth ruadh and back for water, half a day's journey. The custodians recorded it for the three dry years, and then ceased. Known for the walk for water. Told of in: Doire fhionn walks for water (AE 107).

118.note: A great farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The city of the north-west kept a hall of disputation of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. In the forty-ninth year students of Aonghas mac Coinnich carried his question there, why the humans cannot see the colour in broken coal, and the hall argued it until its record ran to four hundred leaves. The last leaf lists those who spoke and notes that the hall adjourned because the peat was done. Known for the four hundred leaves. Told of in: The druid students of Baile Mòr uaine (AE 49); The four hundred leaves come back to Dùn thais (AE 49).

119.note: A harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The harbour town of the eastern shore had carried goods by day along a coast too dangerous to run by night. When Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh was finished in the ninety-first year, A' Chompanaidh's steamers rounded the island without putting in, and the town's coasting boats were laid up within a few years. Voss's white sand came from its dunes. Known for the coasting trade that died. Told of in: Cuan ruadh loses its trade (AE 91).

120.note: A mill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain.

121.note: A mill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean.

122.note: A headland harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. Strake posted constables at the town north of Ros bheag in the last year of the age to hold the coast road, Ceum Ros àrsaidh. The townsfolk brought them food and news, and the news was always a day old. Known for the day-old news. Told of in: Outposts at Ros àrsaidh (AE 150).

124.note: A ford village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean.

125.note: A farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean.

126.note: A village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Headland village with a landing. The fishing town on the southern shore sheltered the crew of A' Chompanaidh's collier when the raiders burned her in the forty-sixth year and set her men rowing for the land; its households fed them until a rider could carry word south. The next year a gunboat of A' Chompanaidh hunted the raiders to a cove near the town and burned every boat drawn up on the shingle, most of them its own fishermen's. The raiders were not found. Known for the burned cove. Told of in: The collier's crew fed near Ceann leathan (AE 46); A cove burned near Ceann leathan (AE 47).

127.note: A hamlet of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The harbour town on Eilean ruadh became in the hundred and twenty-third year the seat of the district of the outer coasts, ruled from its harbour office, where the revenue cutters of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach lay. Its surveyors walked the edge of the great moss beyond the town, found no way across, and left the rest of the district's map blank; the custodians of those coasts were no readier to be counted than the moss. Known for the blank map. Told of in: The district of the outer coasts (AE 123); The blank map of the outer coasts (AE 123).

128.note: A village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. The farming town of the south-east, not the salt port of that name in the west, sent grain to the hills by the eastern roads from the first winter of Cogadh nam Beann, and the council's roll lists the carts; Dùghall of the harbour quarter counted them at Ros dhomhain. Known for the grain carts. Told of in: Grain from Seann Warr (AE 150).

129.note: A hill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha.

130.note: A hill-fort of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean.

131.note: A farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The crews of the northern pit town rose in the same week as the other northern pits in the hundred and forty-ninth year, took the constable posts at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm, and sent the constables south on foot. Their crew-leaders had left a cairn of spoil-stones, one from each pit, on the moor above Cnoc naomh the night they fixed the week. Known for the northern rising. Told of in: The northern pits rise (AE 149).

132.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Ìomhar Seabhag's hawk-shrine, where the hawk company was called. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. The walled harbour of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig heard Murchadh Seabhag preach the hawk's old freedom against the strangers' tithe, and a century later Ìomhar Seabhag's sermons went out from it in copies to the camps and the burial clubs. The hawk-shrines opened again along its bay in the season the fever returned. Its fishing families were proud to the end of the age of having chased A' Chompanaidh's first customs men off their harbour. Murchadh Seabhag preached from the steps of its temple, and copies of his sermons were carried inland to the camps by fishermen. Its harbour was shut to A' Chompanaidh's shipping in the war. Known for the hawk sermons. Told of in: Ìomhar Seabhag (AE 140); The hawk-shrines open (AE 150); Murchadh Seabhag preaches at Seann Skell (AE 22); The hawk sermon carried south in the bird-bags (AE 22).

133.note: A strait harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean.

134.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Farm town with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The harbour town up the western coast heard of Na Trì Longan within two days of their coming, and its custodian rode south to see them. In the first years of the strangers Torcall the mason set a new stone face on its harbour wall, and when a human supply-brig broke on the reefs south of the town its custodian gave the drowned ground above the tide-line among the dunes. The town kept that ground apart for the strangers' dead for the rest of the age. The custodian who rode south in the first year to see the ships wrote the only account of them from the western coast, and it was her successor who asked Torcall to mend the wall. Known for the strangers' graves in the dunes. Told of in: The custodian of Baile fhiadhaich rides south (AE 1); The nine drowned buried on the western shore (AE 6).

135.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the camp of the deep galleries under the hill, houses built of spoil; An Acair Uaine where A' Phlàigh Uaine was first marked; the Sloc Mòr is here. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The large farming village in the deep fields above the workings became a camp when the new galleries were opened into its hill, and it was the worst place on the hill in A' Bhreac Bhallach. Beitris Bhàn laid out its dead at her own table, the washing-women first said there that the girl of the spoil-houses did not grow, and Anne Colby kept her sick-house of canvas there through A' Phlàigh Uaine, which began among its huts. Walter Crane walked its sick-rows. Its granaries fed the camps for a century. The feather Beitris Bhàn nailed over her own door was copied on doors across the camps as fast as the overseers pulled them down, and the roll of the camp keeps the first cases of A' Phlàigh Uaine under her name. Known for the camp where A' Phlàigh Uaine began. Told of in: The camp at Achadh dhomhain (AE 68); The first cases at Achadh dhomhain (AE 73); The pox dead of the hill buried below Achadh dhomhain (AE 39); Beitris Bhàn takes up the laying-out at Achadh dhomhain (AE 68); The nine of the first winter (AE 68); Cormag mac Ailein raises the first house of spoil (AE 68); The women's rule of silence (AE 71).

136.note: A great farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The city of the white sand lay below the dunes of Cuan ruadh. Peter Voss, a glazier of A' Chompanaidh who would not take passage home when his contract ended, built a glass-house there in the sixty-sixth year and melted the sand with charcoal from the hills. His first three firings gave only a black slag that the children carried off for luck; the fourth gave a pale green pane, and his apprentice Cairistìona nic Griogair laughed at the sight of a gull through it. It was the first glass made on Dia-thìr, and the town's apprentices were blowing it without him within a generation. Its custodians were among those of the east whose petitions against the coal tally in the drought went unanswered. Known for the first glass of Dia-thìr. Told of in: Voss stays behind at Baile Mòr dhìreach (AE 65); The glass-house at Baile Mòr dhìreach (AE 66); Cairistìona nic Griogair sees the first pane (AE 66); The first three firings give only slag (AE 66); The tally not lowered (AE 110).

137.note: A mill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The river port just east of the capital argued three days over the war, as much on trade as on loyalty, and then sent its boats to the council at Cathair dhearg. Through that winter and the next the boats carried food down the Abhainn fhionn to the capital by night. Known for the boats sent to the council. Told of in: Muileann mhin takes sides (AE 149).

138.note: A chapel village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean.

139.note: A village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Harbour on an Old Ones' site. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha.

141.note: A village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Chapel village with a landing. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean.

142.note: A town of Cathair gheal: the Dia-thìreach village with the human farms and mill of the concession beside it. In the fiftieth year human farmers of the concession cleared land beside the Tuathaich village of the upland north-west and built a mill; through the first winter the villagers sold them grain at a fair price and carried it on their own ponies, and when the farmers' mill turned in the spring they sold no more and gave no reason. A town of both peoples at the close of the age. Known for the grain sold for one winter. Told of in: Human farms at Cnoc ghorm (AE 50); Cnoc ghorm stops selling grain (AE 50).

143.note: A town of Cathair gheal: a Dia-thìreach harbour with the concession's human fishing families and their tobacco slopes behind it. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The great harbour under the north-western headland took in the first human fishing families of the concession in the fifty-first year, the first humans to fish the island's waters for their own living. Tobacco grew on the concession farms behind it. Manannan's priests kept Oidhche Glaise on its quay, and Ruth Pallant, who taught Hannah Webb the night watch, lived near it. Gorta Baile chrom struck it hard. At the close of the age its harbour officer carried the town's chest of keys two days south to Cuan shean. Its harbour lies under the beacon of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, and in the hunger years it sent what boats it had south along the coast for grain. A town of both peoples at the close of the age. Known for the concession fishers. Told of in: A fishing station at Ceann mhòr (AE 51); Tobacco on the concession farms (AE 52); Manannan's priests on the grey night (AE 133); Ruth Pallant teaches Hannah Webb the night watch (AE 132).

144.note: A farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The quays below Inis bheag on the Abhainn bheag took the eastern coal that Inis bheag could not load. Its townsfolk were paid by the barge, and with the gain the town built its first stone houses. Known for its first stone houses. Told of in: Baile mhin ships the eastern coal (AE 54).

145.note: A field village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The village in the hills north of the workings kept Na Seann Spioradan, and its households would not light their hearths with coal bought of A' Chompanaidh; they burned peat as their grandparents had, and their elders taught that coal burned for wages was burned twice. Fionnghal nic Artair rode there in an Giblean of the twenty-third year and read her letter in defence of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig at the hearth of Sìleas nic Uilleim. Asked what burned on her own hearth, she answered bought coal, and was sent home with thanks. Known for the hearths that burned no bought coal. A' Chompanaidh forbade coal to be left lying and had the offerings gathered up. The search party that went up after the surveyors came back with nothing but the tale of the Marbh-bheò. 152.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. A' Chompanaidh's second coal port, end of the mule tram-road. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The harbour on the straight headland of the gulf became A' Chompanaidh's second coal port in the seventieth year, to carry off the yield of the southern workings without the long haul round to Ros dhomhain. Edward Vane laid an iron tram-road drawn by mules from the pits down to its quay; it halved the cost of shipping coal and ended the carting trade of the villages on the old road. A' Phlàigh Uaine fell on it among the first of the coast towns. It is the harbour of Cnoc mhòr's cattle trade, and the drovers kept their own quay beside A' Chompanaidh's coal stage for the whole of the age. Known for the tram-road and the second coal stage. Told of in: Ros dhìreach the second coal port (AE 70); The tram-road to Ros dhìreach (AE 115); The wreck off Ros dhìreach (AE 70).

The river port east of the capital on the Abhainn fhionn took An Scàird Fhuilteach from the coal barges in the sixtieth year, after a sick bargeman was put ashore there. Its custodians, led by Mairead nic Amhlaidh, shut the only barge landing the town had for a whole season, though it cost every fee the landing had ever earned; A' Chompanaidh fined the town for the lost fees, and Mairead read the letter to the council on the landing steps within sight of that season's graves. Known for the shut landing. 163.note: A ford village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The ford town east of the capital is where Rathad na Mèinne crossed the river before climbing into the hills. In the spring of the hundred and forty-ninth year Major Peter Ashdown turned his relief column north about An Taigh-seinnse Mòr to cross there, and met the crews of Baile thais dug in along the willow scrub of the far bank. His column went into the ford waist-high and in poor order, lost forty men to the river and the fire and all its baggage, and went back. The old field of battle at Muileann ghlas lies to its south-west. A' Chompanaidh's baggage abandoned on the near bank went up the hill road on the rebels' carts that night. Known for the fight at the ford. Told of in: Rathad na Mèinne (AE 34); The fight at the ford of Àth chiar (AE 149); The turnip cart to the ford (AE 149).

164.note: A grove village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The carters of the village on the road just east of the capital banded together in the thirty-fifth year to bargain with A' Chompanaidh over the rates for hauling coal, the first Dia-thìreach guild of the age; A' Chompanaidh bought it, because that was cheaper than breaking it. Pàdraig mac Artair, who married Seònaid Bhàn of Cuan chrom, was a carter of the town, and its carters swore at Seònaid's table. Known for the first carters' guild. Told of in: The carters of Doire chaol (AE 35).

The walled temple city of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west declined in the first years to join the joint council of Baile dhìreach, a few miles off, its custodian writing that one town may be a trial but two would be a rule. In the war its priests heard Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe's letter and would send no men, since that was not what Òrd na Cloiche was for, but shut the harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships and opened an Fhianna's roads to the hawk-faithful. Its temple of Lia Fàil, the stone that cries out, is the chief house of Òrd na Cloiche, and its priests keep a driftwood fire that burns blue-white with the salt. Known for the harbour shut in the war. Told of in: Inis thais declines the compact (AE 6); The Leaden Hawk at Inis thais (AE 150); The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the letter (AE 150).

They could be raised no way but by selling boats: eleven of its two-and-twenty went to A' Chompanaidh at its own asking price, and the men who sailed them went into the pits under the next year's contracts. 202.note: A mill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The mill on the deep race grew rich carrying grain to the camps. When the crews brought to break the strike at Cnoc chaol were marched through it, its townsfolk turned them from every door, and they slept in A' Chompanaidh's barns; several went home the next season. After Scàineadh Cill ghlas its custodians met the people of the closed district on the moor road and lent them common ground, on which they built Achadh chaol. It is the seat of its province, and its custodians had long kept the right of the old roads to shelter any traveller who asked; they held that right did not reach men sent to take other men's work. The weavers stopped bringing wool to the humans' market and loaded it for their own crossing instead, and A' Chompanaidh, holding the only deep-water berths on that coast, let it lie until the moths had most of it. 209.note: A grove village of Cathair gheal. The grey oak grove of Coimhdeach na Fine stood in the hunger's country. In the winter of the ninety-fifth year the hunger took its old and its very young first, its custodian walked door to door to write who still stood, and in the spring the village sent its young folk south to the camps for A' Chompanaidh's ration; by the year's end it was half empty. Some of its men had dug for Lowe on A' Chompanaidh's winter wage. Its grove was cut for the camps' timber in the famine years, and those who went south to the camps did not, most of them, come back. 241.note: A farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The farming town of the east lost its seed corn in the ground in the forty-eighth year and borrowed seed from A' Chompanaidh's store at Seann Dunn, to be paid back in grain over five harvests. Tormod mac Pheadair, keeper of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg and kin of the town by marriage, walked there to read the terms to its council figure by figure. The custodians entered the debt under the night of the moon with its measure and its five harvests, the first debt in grain to the strangers in any roll of the island. Known for the first debt in grain. Told of in: Tormod mac Pheadair reads the seed loan at Baile ruadh (AE 48); Baile ruadh loses its seed (AE 48); Baile ruadh's seed debt entered (AE 48).

242.note: A field village of Cathair gheal. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The field village on the far western shore sent out the boats that first met Na Trì Longan, under the steersman Lachlann Odhar, who sent word home and went on south to Cuan shean. Its people told the story of that morning longer than any roll kept it, and they fished the same waters under Uilebheist na Mara through all the years the strangers held the coast. Gorta Baile chrom that began in the north-west in the ninety-fourth year, reached it in its second winter and emptied many of its houses, and in the drought years a decade after it was named among the ten districts of the drought country. The houses stand close to the sea-wall, and the steersman's boat was kept drawn up on the shingle under them for as long as anyone remembered whose it had been. Known for the boats that met the strangers. Told of in: The word brought home to Achadh àrsaidh (AE 1); Lachlann Odhar leads the ships down the coast (AE 1).

246.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the cellars of the custodians' rolls, beyond Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's reach; the rolls of the age sent here at the war's end; Sloinneadh Aisling found. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The narrow mill town in the eastern hills held, in the cellar under its mill house, the copies of the custodians' rolls that Na Trì Teaghlaichean of the town made fair winter after winter, the fullest record of the eastern hills and the one no stranger's eye was meant to read. Gormshuil nic Fhearchair was called back from it to the council in the first years, and the rubbing of the first mark went to its loft. Seònag Bhàn kept the copying until her eyes failed, and Cailean mac Eachainn took up the hand at four-and-twenty; it was there he found Sloinneadh Aisling and there, in the last days of the hundred and fiftieth year, that the four chests of the age's rolls came down to him by cart. The copying was done at a long table under a single window, and every copy was made twice, so that no one fire or flood could take the only record of a town. Known for the cellar of copied rolls. Told of in: The custodians' rolls at Muileann chaol (AE 124); The Line of Aisling found (AE 126); The rolls sent to Muileann chaol (AE 150); Gormshuil called back from Muileann chaol (AE 8); Fionnan's birth reaches the cellar (AE 121); Cailean mac Eachainn taken on at the cellar (AE 122); The count of the people copied in the cellar (AE 122); The cellar comes to know the eastern hills by heart (AE 124).

Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The fortified city on the crooked hill commands the roads south of the capital. Its rope-walks, which had spun cable for the fishing boats, turned wholly to winding-rope for the pit-heads in the thirty-first year, and the town grew by half on A' Chompanaidh's pay. A barracks was built there in the years of the constables. When Ashdown's column fell back through it after the ford at Àth chiar, the town shut its gates on the soldiers in the barracks and kept the column's wounded to nurse or to bury. Its citadel commands the roads south of the capital, and the barracks it housed were empty at the close of the age. Known for winding-rope, and the gates shut on Ashdown. Raghnall asked three times for timber at the heading before the roof came down. The road around Doire mhòr was cut through its ground, and A' Chompanaidh's huts followed. The wall of its old heading still stood above the camp at the close of the age, and the crews would not work the gallery beneath it. Known for the Eleven. 282.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Where the humans first came ashore and whence the last Àrd-mhaor sailed; its custodians shut the harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The old harbour of the west was the first town of Dia-thìr to see the strangers, when Na Trì Longan lay off its cape in the first year and their people spent forty days on the dunes below it while the council decided what to do with them. Oighrig nic Leòid, its custodian, gave them water before any vote allowed it. The humans prayed in one of its sail-lofts in those first winters, and Fiabhras nan Coigreach went out from its quays into the country. For a hundred years coal came down to it from the hill and went out in the humans' hulls. In the last autumn of the age its custodians shut the harbour to every ship of A' Chompanaidh, and it was from its quay that Lionel Strake sailed, with three chests of harbour keys set at his feet. In the siege year it was the one western harbour that answered neither side's letters. Known for the first landing, and the last ship. The fishing town on the eastern cape kept a driftwood fire to bring its boats home in a storm long before the strangers came, and Torcall Clachair laid his second cairn there in the sixth year with James Fenn beside him. When A' Chompanaidh raised Taigh-solais Baile ìseal in the twenty-seventh year, the lime for its mortar was burned on the shore with coal carted over the hills from Muileann chrom, and the keeping of the lamp went to the fishing households, who drew lots for the watches at Samhain as they had for the fire. The custodians won a rule that the lamp be lowered on the nights the boats went to the deep grounds, and the old fire was still lit beside the tower. Known for the fire beside the beacon. The villages of the south sent meal north to the hill villages in the hungry thirty-first year, as the custom of An Aois Naomh bids. The agents of A' Chompanaidh at Àth ìseal bought two of the nine carts on the road; the seven that refused their marks went on into the hills and gave their meal away sack by sack at the village doors, as Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte bids, and their drivers came home by the carriers' road with their carts empty. The long walled city of the south follows Macha, and its oak woods had been cut for A' Chompanaidh's pit-props since the first contracts. The age's rolls note the day the last oak of its own cutting came down, and the priests of Macha who would not stand for the blessing of the coin were many of them its people. Its priests of Macha were the first to refuse to stand for the blessing of the humans' coin in the capital's temple, and many of them followed the dissenters to the forest. Known for the oaks that went for pit-props. 301.note: A strait harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The small harbour on the northern coast took in the crew of a brig of A' Chompanaidh wrecked in sea mist off Eilean fhada in the fifty-fifth year; they waded ashore at low water and walked there. A' Chompanaidh built a quay at the town for the eastern trade, and by the hundred and forty-fifth year it saw one ship in a season. Its agent wrote to Ros dhomhain that he had been forgotten, and no answer came back to him that Rathad na Mèinne ever heard of. Known for the forgotten agent. Told of in: A brig lost in the mist (AE 55); Caol bheag's empty quay (AE 145); The forgotten agent of Caol bheag (AE 145).

303.note: A town of Cathair gheal: the greatest town of the north-west, named in the truce to receive the columns; its Dia-thìrich given the choice of staying or going south. The red walled city of the north-west, the greatest town of that country, had lived under the humans' governance longer than any other on the island. The truce named it the place where the columns would be received, and its own Dia-thìrich folk were given the choice, at a gathering in the market square, of staying under the truce or going south. The roll set the two numbers side by side, and they were close. It was held by Dia-thìreach lords from An Aois Naomh, and the humans' magistrates sat in its hall for most of the age. Known for the choice put to its people. Told of in: Baile Mòr ruadh receives the columns (AE 150).

304.note: A town of Cathair gheal: the truce was agreed here, on the edge of the concession. The ancient ford in the north-west, on the edge of the country the humans first settled, is where the envoys of the council and of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach met in its meeting-house in the last week of an Dàmhair of the hundred and fiftieth year, with two scribes writing the same words in two hands, and agreed the truce: the humans to withdraw into the north-west under safe-conduct, and the towns of that country to be left standing. The meeting-house has a single long table down its middle, and both copies of the truce were signed at it on the third day. Known for the truce. Told of in: The truce of Àth àrsaidh (AE 150); Two scribes, one truce (AE 150).

305.note: A town of Cathair gheal: the hunger was worst here, within sight of the new beacon; Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's kitchen; the human labourers' vigil of the Grey Night in the fields near it. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The bent town on the far north-western coast stands beside Taigh-solais Baile chrom, the last of the five lights built and the first as the ring is counted. Uisdean mac Lachlainn kept it from its lighting in the ninety-first year and his son Lachlann after him, and the daybook there first wrote the three words *Cha tàinig long*. Gorta Baile chrom, took its name from the town in the ninety-fourth year. Hannah Webb kept her night vigil in the fields behind it from the hundred and thirty-third year, and Am Fiabhras Glas settled hardest round it. Lachlann watched the last Àrd-mhaor's ship stand out past its headland. An Togail that built its tower was set aside in the famine districts in the hunger years, too late for the harvest, and never used again. Known for its light, and Gorta Baile chrom. Told of in: Baile chrom goes hungry (AE 94); The relief ship (AE 96); A grey-night vigil at Baile chrom (AE 133); Baile chrom's condition for the fifth cairn (AE 6); The fire on the north-west headland raised for Fenn (AE 6); The draft read at Baile chrom (AE 92); The first harvest short (AE 93); Uisdean begins to write beyond the weather (AE 94).

306.note: A farm town of Cathair gheal. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The Tuathaich town sent forty-one of its people to the pits under An Togail, the largest tally of any single town. 308.note: A well village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig. The village of the grasslands in the western hills lay off every road but the one from Ros bheag to the northern concession. In the last year of the age the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lay eleven hours in the long grass above that road and counted every rider who passed, Gillebrìde keeping the tally on a strip of bark: forty-one constables' riders in a day, all going south and none north. Known for the count in the grass. Told of in: The watch in the grasslands (AE 150); Eleven hours in the grass above Tobar dhomhain (AE 150); Forty-one riders, all going south (AE 150).

311.note: A farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The cattle town of the east had no grazing left within four days' driving in the second summer of Tiormachd Achadh shean, and its custodian Ealasaid Ruadh ordered the whole herd killed and salted rather than lose it on the road. The salt meat was sold to A' Chompanaidh for the camps at a price A' Chompanaidh named. The town lost fewer of its people to hunger that winter than any other in the drought country. Known for the herd salted. Told of in: The cattle of Baile chaol (AE 107); Baile chaol slaughters its herd (AE 107).

313.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean, known for its coal stage shelled by a steamship of A' Chompanaidh from the river and the fishing town behind it set burning; twenty-three dead. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The old river port in the hollow of the rock was made a coal landing early in the age, and its barge-stage took the hill's coal down the Abhainn uaine for more than a century. In the first winter of the war a ship of A' Chompanaidh came up the river and shelled the stage to keep it from the rebels; three-and-twenty of the fishing town behind it died, and the ship burned island coal to do it. Its walls follow Macha. Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe passed the burned stage on the first day of their walk north and found a woman sorting stone from ash with her bare hands at what had been her hearth. Known for the shelling of the coal stage. Told of in: Seann Toll made a coal landing (AE 35); Seann Toll shelled (AE 150); The letter read at a nameless hawk-house (AE 150).

315.note: A hill-fort of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The low fort-city of the east, an hour's walk from the silver town, kept a small constable post from the years of the constables. Cut off by the rising, it yielded to Comann an Airgid's riflemen after a single exchange of fire, and the whole east of the island stood clear of human arms. The old walls of Talla na Lasrach stand at it, where the keeper of the flame once settled the silver quarrel of the guild by giving each side half. Known for the post that yielded. Told of in: The surrender at Dùn ìseal (AE 150).

The holy hill south of the capital laid the dead of A' Phlàigh Uaine in its shrine's burial ground until it was full, and then in the field beside it, which was never ploughed again. In the months before the rising the crew-leaders of the north met by night on the moor above it and raised a cairn of spoil-stones from their own pits; the nineteen dead of the ford at Àth chiar were buried within sight of it. It has been a house of Macha since An Aois Scaraidh, and lies close by the old battlefield of Muileann ghlas. Known for the unploughed field and the two cairns. 327.note: A mill village of Cathair gheal. The small mill town on the north coast stands beside Taigh-solais Muileann bheag, the only one of the five lights to burn coal. Its keeper Ailig mac Griogair asked three winters running to go back to the old lamp, and its fishermen complained that the colour the coal flame cast on the water drove the herring off. Lowe came to see the flame and the keeper's son answered him on the point. Within a season the herring came back, and the complaint was withdrawn. In the stoppage of the hundred and forty-third year its pits stopped with the rest. The coal flame's colour on the water was still remarked by every stranger who passed the cape at night. Known for the coal-burning light. It had been a gathering place for the drovers of the north since before the strangers came, and the fields where the columns camped were grazing again by the spring. Known for the name written down. 351.note: A town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. A' Chompanaidh's coal quay, seized by the crews and its mouth blocked with two sunk barges. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The long spit on the Abhainn uaine, a short hour's walk under Doire mhòr, held its foreshore in common, and A' Chompanaidh's first surveyors found it covered with their own men. A' Chompanaidh built its coal quay there, and for a century barges loaded the hill's coal for the coast. On the first day of the rising the crews took the quay and sank two loaded barges across its mouth; the boatman Pàdraig Reamhar knocked the plugs from a hull he had built with his own father. No coal left the hills by water again in the age. Its pilots guided A' Chompanaidh's barges through the shoals below the spit for a century, and the rivalry with Inis ìseal downstream went on untouched by all of it. Known for the barges sunk across its quay. 354.note: A city of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the heart of A' Chompanaidh's pits: overseers' town, weigh-house burned, the store taken at first light by Mòrag nic Iain's crews; Slighe a' Ghuail runs from here. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The mill on the bend of the river is the heart of the coal country. Six sacks of its hill's coal went down to the strangers in the first years, and the first contract was read aloud at the mill. Raghnall mac Dhòmhnaill took A' Chompanaidh's staff here and a house with a slate roof, and his son Dòmhnall, his grandson Iain and his great-granddaughter Mòrag held it after him, until Mòrag broke it across her knee on A' Chompanaidh's step in the hundred and forty-eighth year. Seven men drowned in its flooded gallery, and the inquiry struck her testimony out. On the twenty-eighth of an Gearran in the hundred and forty-ninth year its people took the walled store at first light, and the war began here. Its mill still ground grain for the central country through all the years of the coal, and the steelyard ledgers of its weigh-house, in which the hill's coal had been set down by the ton since the first contract, burned green in the ledger fires of the hundred and fiftieth year. Known for the overseer's staff, and the first morning of the war. It lived on the carrying trade between the two. It began as a coal-breaking mill for the diggings in the hills east of the capital, and the carters of both towns shared one inn and one quarrel for the rest of the age. It was the first order of his rule the Dia-thìrich approved, and they said so. Its quays stand on Eilean chrom across the strait, and the physician's boat went out from them to every ship that came in under the quarantine. Known for the quarantine station. 383.note: A large village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. A' Chompanaidh's camp of timber huts at the ford below the new workings, the first settlement made for the pit alone. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The low ford below the new workings became the first of A' Chompanaidh's camps: timber huts where the ferrymen had always put the carts across in the wet season, and a store of A' Chompanaidh where the clerk had no book for cheese. The families who came down from Doire mhòr and the hill villages went to its huts, and A' Bhreac Bhallach and the fever were worst among them. Its roll was the one in which the line of Aisling was first found. The ford floods every wet season and the ferrymen still put the carts across, and the camp grew into a town of rows beside the old crossing. Its chaplain in A' Bhreac Bhallach wrote every dead man, woman and child in a fair hand. Known for A' Chompanaidh's first camp. 387.note: A great farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The walled city of red stone suffered worst from the fever of foul water that followed the drought into the towns, for its wells had been deepened into the old middens; seventeen died. Coll, Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's young physician there, tested the water and was the first to name the cause rightly. Its citadel is the strongest place of its province, and after the drought its custodians had the old midden ground walled off and the wells sunk anew outside it. Known for Coll's report on the water. Its shrine-keepers lit a new lamp without the old keeper's name on it. It stands on the edge of the fenced ground, and from its well the wire of the closed district can be seen along the slope. Known for a village built without a surveyor. Told of in: Achadh chaol raised by the dispossessed (AE 137); Achadh chaol's first roll opened (AE 138).

In the hills beyond the capital, the guards of A' Chompanaidh and the constables sallying from the capital's harbour to win back the eastern road were driven back at the town in the last year of the age, in Blàr Cnoc ghorm. It was the last attempt Riaghaltas nan Coigreach made in the war to reach the mining district. Known for Blàr Cnoc ghorm. Told of in: The fight at Cnoc ghorm (AE 150).

393.note: A ford village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The grey ford beside Cathair mhòr is remembered for Sìne Ruadh, custodian in A' Phlàigh Uaine, who ordered every hut where a death had been burned with its bedding. A' Chompanaidh protested the loss of its property, and the custodians noted that the sickness stopped sooner at Àth ghlas than anywhere else. The story was still told by grandparents in the fever years sixty years later. It lies a short way from the ruin of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, which is older than any dwelling of the Dia-thìrich, and the huts it burned were never rebuilt on the same ground. Known for the burning of the huts. Told of in: Sìne Ruadh orders the huts of Àth ghlas burned (AE 73); Àth ghlas burns its huts (AE 74).

395.note: A field village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The granary of the east keeps the shared-meal custom of An Aois Naomh. In the years before the war Faire nan Lòchran's ledgers of the money it had from Comann an Airgid were kept in the roof-space of its shrine, above the rafters, and no clerk of A' Chompanaidh ever thought to look for them there. It is one of the largest settlements on the island though it is still called a field village, and its grain went to the capital in the siege year. Known for the ledgers in the shrine roof. Told of in: The Sligeanach's psalter (AE 142); Achadh mhòr keeps the ledgers (AE 143).

398.note: A well village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Bhrìde. Its first keeper was chosen by Riaghaltas nan Coigreach on the custodians' word. In the first spring of the war its keeper Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill put the light out with her own hand, before any order reached her, rather than guide A' Chompanaidh's ships along a coast the council held; when the truce was signed the council had it lit again. The keeper's daybook there ends its entries for the war with a line of Raonaid's own, and takes them up again without comment at the relighting. Known for the light put out in the war. 411.note: A field village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The old field gave its name to Tiormachd Achadh shean, which lay on the east from the hundred and sixth year to the hundred and tenth. Its wells failed a month before any other, its custodian wrote to Iseabail nic Leòid at Àth mhòr twice a week, and in the third year Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise sank deep wells there with a boring-rig from an Tìr Thall, and they held. The custodians set Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's wells and A' Chompanaidh's tallies on facing pages without comment. It stands at the heart of the farming country south and east of the cape, and in the first dry year its custodian wrote that the granaries of the old custom would carry them through the winter, which they did, once. Known for Tiormachd Achadh shean and Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's wells. The drovers' town at the bent ford was one of the two where Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise sank deep wells in the drought years, and they held. In the last weeks of the age its custodians stood at the ford and counted the columns over, family by family, from first light until past noon; it was the last count the Dia-thìrich made of the humans on Dia-thìr in the age. Its people are drovers, and the ford is crossed by the drove road north. Known for the last count. Told of in: The columns at Àth chrom (AE 150).

415.note: A hill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The narrow hill was a mining camp worked by night crews in the last decades of the age. Griogair mac Ailein died in A' Chompanaidh's lock-up there, held for a short-weighted cartload he did not cut, and Thomas Hale came to read the surgeon's note over his grave. The day shift stood in the yard in silence for the night crews, Faire nan Lòchran's purse ran dry keeping the strikers fed, and the strike was broken by crews brought in through Muileann dhomhain. Grodadh nan Scamhan was worse there than on any other hill. In the hundred and forty-eighth year its overseer threw down his staff in the week Mòrag broke hers. Its crews were among the first to work by the clay lamps of Baile ghorm, and the pithead there was lit all night from the year the night shift began. Known for Stad-oibre Cnoc chaol. 418.note: A harbour of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The ford town on the northern road kept a carters' house at its quay that stood roofless for most of the age. Muireall nic Fhearchair, carrying her aunt's papers east to the loft at Muileann chaol in the thirtieth year, was held there by rain and read Clàr nan Dà Fhichead Dath aloud to the carters. That same autumn the town's carter, Seònaid Bhàn's father, lodged the drivers and oxen of the meal-carts of Doire fhiadhaich. Seònaid married Pàdraig mac Artair of Doire chaol there, took the old carters' house, and made her rule of marks and barter at its table. Known for Seònaid Bhàn's table. 419.note: A town of Comann an Airgid. Comann an Airgid's town under Cùmhnant an Airgid; rose for the council and escorted A' Chompanaidh's agents to the coast. The silver town lies in the far east of the hills on a shelf of the valley under the moor, an hour's walk from the old walls at Dùn ìseal. Its guild, Comann an Airgid, held its seam under a compact that Ùna locked in the guild chest in the first half-century, and the surveyors who came for its ledgers were turned back at the adit. The guild sent its bar to the sea by Seann Bhral rather than A' Chompanaidh's quays, paid for the mark in silver, refused Martha Gale's partnership in the sixty-seventh year by a count of hands in its hall, and in the years before the war bought rifles from the raiders of the eastern waters and entered them in its ledger as refining tools. In the rising its riflemen took Dùn ìseal and cleared the east of human arms. The seam is silver near the great vein but not of it. Catrìona nic Eachainn, a refiner of the guild, died there an old woman in the hundred and fourth year, and Ùna nic Choinnich headed the guild into her eightieth winter. Known for the guild compact and its riflemen. Told of in: The Silver Compact (AE 44); Muileann chiar grows (AE 81); The silver town rises (AE 150); Ùna nic Choinnich calls the guild to the hall (AE 43); The guild asks for the compact in both tongues (AE 43); The compact read in the guild hall (AE 44); The guild's book of weighings filled (AE 44); Ùna locks the compact in the guild chest (AE 45); The guild enters the Baile gheal salt in its ledger (AE 45).

420.note: A farm town of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The coastal town a day's walk up from Cuan shean took Fiabhras nan Coigreach in the tenth year, which killed its custodian and both her sons, though no human dwelt in the town at all. The custodians of the west took note of it. Known for the fever without strangers. Told of in: The fever at Baile àrsaidh (AE 10).

422.note: A hill-fort of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. The red hill-fort of the east sent Fionnghal nic Artair to Cathair dhearg in the early years, and hers is the only defence of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig that survives from the time it went out; the council filed her letter. The city kept its own counsel through the age. In the war its custodians sent grain south and read their declaration from the steps of the hall, quoting her sentence a hundred and twenty-seven years after she wrote it. The mills of Muileann dhomhain ground its bread and its custodians sent grain west to the camps in the hunger years by the old custom, asking nothing for it. Known for Fionnghal's letter, read again in the war. Told of in: Half of Dùn dhearg comes to the board (AE 21); The counter of Dùn dhearg dies (AE 21); A defence of the Law at Dùn dhearg (AE 22); Fionnghal nic Artair rides to Cathair dhearg (AE 22); The custodian of Dùn dhearg goes back to peat (AE 24); Dùn dhearg declares (AE 150).
