The walled town of Òrd na Cloiche, where Imrich nam Pantar passes, did in the first fever years what the hills only talked of: it turned the fever back at its gates. Riaghaltas nan Coigreach fined it for hindering trade, and it paid the fine in wool, more sacks than the humans knew what to do with. Its priests kept the oldest shrines of Òrd na Cloiche open through all the age. Its wool fine was long told in the south-west as the one bargain the humans ever lost by weight. 436.note: A ford village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The town of the eastern drought country was kept through Tiormachd Achadh shean by its custodian Iseabail nic Leòid. In the hundred and seventh year she drove the herds of Àth mhòr and Achadh shean a day west to the tarn above Doire fhionn, and fewer than half the beasts reached water on their own legs; she kept a count of the fallen, ninety-eight marks. Of the ten drought custodians who petitioned Haskins, each unknown to the others, she rode her own petition to Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, and over the following winter wrote forty pages on the three dry years. Haskins answered in two lines, and a later clerk bound the two together. Known for the forty pages. A second constable post was raised there in the hundred and thirty-third year near the northern workings; its custodian was paid rent for the ground, and with it bought the village out of its debts to A' Chompanaidh's store. The post fell with Muileann shean's in the first week of the rising. The humans' wool-buyers came to its fairs every year of the age, and paid in marks once the coin was struck. 461.note: A chapel village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhacha. The temple village of Macha at the edge of the workings kept a small shrine where the pit crews left the first piece of coal from every new gallery. A' Chompanaidh suffered the custom, since it cost a stone a gallery, and the shrine was one of the two pit-mouth shrines where the crews kept the old words of the rock face in the strangers' years. It lies beside Ceann leathan, where the old contest is still held each year, and its druids tended the shrine through the whole of the age without a quarrel of A' Chompanaidh. Its post as custodian Coinneach Ruadh kept eleven years before the petition, and he went on keeping it after he lost the clerkship. Known for the eleven who signed. 476.note: A town of Cathair gheal: the human market town of the concession, with its magistrate's stone hall and chapel; it kept its gates and militia out of the war. The walled city of white stone on the far western coast was a Dia-thìreach town until the human families of the northern concession made it their market in the fiftieth year. Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise kept a chapel and, in the fever years, a hospital where Dia-thìrich and human sick lay side by side for the first time because there was no longer room to keep them apart; Hannah Webb nursed in its wards. In the war it shut its gates, raised a militia that went nowhere, and its magistrate asked both sides to be left alone. Its harbour officer rode south with his town's keys at the end. Obadiah Renn, the minister of Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise, sat with Hannah Webb in the chapel over her vigil, and wrote of it to Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise's house at Cathair dhearg. Known for the concession's market and the shared wards. 489.note: A city of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean: the hawk company mustered here and held the road from Ros bheag to the north-west. Its people keep the rite of Òrd Mhanannain. The great river port of the west, a short march north-east of Ros bheag, was where the company of the hawk-faithful mustered under Ìomhar Seabhag's eye in the early summer of the hundred and fiftieth year, and where the seven of Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe were told they were one company with one name. The company held the road between Ros bheag and the north-west for the rest of the war. It is the largest place on the island after the capital, and its barges run down the Abhainn naomh to Ros àrsaidh. Known for the hawk company's muster. 491.note: A mill village of Comhairle nan Coimheadaichean. Its people keep the rite of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean. The mill town a short way from Cill ghlas was where Griogair mac Aonghais told Fearchar Bard to sing the song that went round every pit of the hills without his name on it. In the three years before the rising the smith Uilleam Gobha turned A' Chompanaidh's blasting-powder, bought a keg at a time on a chit of A' Chompanaidh, into bombs packed in tin from the coal sheds' scrap, and forged pike-heads by day out of rail-iron; the rebels' council wrote that without his forge the rising could not have been fought past its first weeks. Taigh na Fèithe above the town kept Leabhar a' Chùraim of the hill through the long centuries, and its keepers set down A' Chompanaidh's coming in the same hand as everything before it. Known for Uilleam Gobha's forge. Theirs was the one craft of the island sold across the sea under its own name. It stands at the meeting of Rathad na Mèinne and the mills with a citadel above it, and its smiths' marks were known in the humans' shops across the sea. Known for its silversmiths. add.name: Slighe a' Ghuail
add.note: A' Chompanaidh's railway from the pits at Muileann chrom by Cathair dhearg to the deep-water quay at Ros dhomhain (AE 120); broken in three places in the war, mended by the kingdom in SE 8. Told of in: The coal line (AE 120); The coal line repaired (SE 8).

add.name: the mule tram-road to Ros dhìreach
add.note: Vane's iron tram-road drawn by mules from the southern workings down to the coal port (AE 115); left to the mules when Slighe a' Ghuail opened. Told of in: The tram-road to Ros dhìreach (AE 115); The coal line (AE 120).

add.name: the eastern Rathad na Mèinne
add.note: Coal from the eastern workings carted over the rebuilt Drochaid Ros fhionn to the river quays of Inis bheag and Baile mhin; fallen silent since the eastern pits flooded in the war. Told of in: Drochaid Ros fhionn (AE 53); Coal through Inis bheag (AE 53); Baile mhin ships the eastern coal (AE 54); The eastern pits at Ros fhionn (AE 150).

add.name: the coal barges of the Abhainn uaine
add.note: The barges from the landing at Seann Toll and Cidhe Beag down to Ceann leathan, where A' Chompanaidh's ships loaded; no coal has left the hills by water since the quay at Ceann fhada was seized. Told of in: Barges at Cidhe Beag (AE 32); Seann Toll made a coal landing (AE 35); The coal ships' lane (AE 36); The quay at Ceann fhada seized (AE 149).

add.name: A' Chompanaidh cart-road round Doire mhòr
add.note: Run round the fields of Doire mhòr and not through them, to the working at Cnoc fhiadhaich. Told of in: The road around Doire mhòr (AE 15).

add.name: the road of the columns north
add.note: The human families marched north along the western roads under guard of Buidhnean na Comhairle; counted over at the ford of Àth chrom, camped a night at Àth leathan. Told of in: The columns go north (AE 150); The columns at Àth chrom (AE 150); Àth leathan (AE 150).

0.note: Through the mining camps and along the coal roads; twenty-six settlements had cases. Told of in: A' Phlàigh Uaine (AE 73); The first cases at Achadh dhomhain (AE 73); Twenty-six settlements (AE 74).

1.note: Thirty-four settlements; worse because An Togail had taken the hands. Told of in: Gorta Baile chrom (AE 94); Baile chrom goes hungry (AE 94); The famine country (AE 94).

2.note: Three dry years; the custodians counted ten districts of the east. Told of in: Tiormachd Achadh shean (AE 106); The wells of Achadh shean (AE 107); The dry country (AE 107).

3.note: A' Chompanaidh fenced the district and left it to the thorn. Told of in: Scàineadh Cill ghlas (AE 137); The district closed (AE 137).

add.name: the northern concession (AE 20)
add.note: Upland pasture about Muileann àrsaidh for human families who would not work in the pits. Told of in: The northern concession (AE 20).

add.name: An Togail country (AE 88–97)
add.note: One in five of the able grown folk of the western and northern villages sent to the pits for two years; set aside too late for the harvest. Told of in: The Levy (AE 88); The Levy in the north-west (AE 88); The Levy set aside (AE 97).

add.name: the lines at midsummer AE 150
add.note: The council held the hills, the east and the capital; Strake held Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, the harbour quarter below it and the western ports. Told of in: The lines at midsummer (AE 150).

add.name: the mining country of the rising (AE 149)
add.note: Where the war opened: Muileann chrom, Ceann fhada, Baile thais, the northern pits. Told of in: War (AE 149); The stores taken at Muileann chrom (AE 149); The quay at Ceann fhada seized (AE 149); The siege of the store at Baile thais (AE 149); The northern pits rise (AE 149).

add.name: the lifted Ceò Mhanannain (AE 1)
add.note: The mist that lay on the eastern sea since a' Scaradh lifted from the northern water in the winter of An t-Aiseag. Told of in: The ships met off the north-west (AE 1).

add.name: Ros fhionn
add.note: Ground the sea has taken. Told of in: The camp at Achadh dhomhain (AE 68); The eastern pits at Ros fhionn (AE 150).
The iron bird (burned). Told of in: The iron bird (AE 147); The harbour quarter changes sides (AE 150).
